The newly hatched yolk-sac larva of the Sand steenbras (Lithognathus mormyrus) emerges from the chorion at a remarkably small size, measuring a total length of only 0.174 cm [Lb = 0.174 cm] at the moment of eclosion. This initial body length is accompanied by an extraordinarily low wet weight of 0.0001 g [Wwb = 0.0001 g], reflecting the minimal maternal investment in the individual offspring characteristic of many broadcast-spawning sparids that produce large numbers of pelagic eggs. The lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during this early phase, which progresses rapidly under warm incubation conditions. Experimental rearing studies conducted at a controlled temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] have documented that the period from fertilization to the point of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of first exogenous feeding spans approximately 1.667 days [ab = approximately 1.667 days]. This brief pre-feeding interval, lasting less than two full days, underscores the species’ need for a productive planktonic environment immediately following the transition to active feeding, as the tiny larvae must begin capturing prey quickly before their finite energy stores are exhausted.

As the post-larval transformation progresses, the juvenile Sand steenbras undergoes a substantial morphological and physiological transition. The age at which individuals first reach reproductive maturity, defined here as the first spawning event, has been documented in laboratory populations maintained at a stable 23 °C [T = 23 °C] to be 623.2 days after hatching [tR = 623.2 days after hatching]. This relatively delayed onset of reproduction, occurring at just over 1.7 years after hatching, is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy that prioritizes the accumulation of body mass before diverting resources toward gametogenesis. At the point of first reproduction, the total length of the fish averages 15.48 cm [Lp = 15.48 cm], indicating that a substantial body size must be achieved before the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis triggers the complex process of vitellogenesis and spermiation. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental milestone is 45.39 g [Wwp = 45.39 g], a value that reflects the somatic investment required to reach the size threshold associated with successful spawning in coastal waters.

The maximum reproductive output of the Sand steenbras occurs under optimal thermal conditions, with field and laboratory data converging on an estimate for the peak daily spawning rate at a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. Under this thermal regime, a sexually mature adult female can release, on average, approximately 1137.53 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1137.53 eggs per day], a fecundity that positions this species among the more prolific iteroparous spawners within the family Sparidae. This high daily egg production is facilitated by a group-synchronous ovarian organization, wherein oocytes at various stages of vitellogenesis are present simultaneously, allowing for successive spawning events across an extended breeding season. The 19 °C temperature is not an arbitrary threshold; it corresponds closely to the mean sea surface temperature recorded during the peak spawning months in the Mediterranean and along the eastern Atlantic coast, suggesting a tight evolutionary coupling between thermal physiology and reproductive phenology. Higher temperatures are associated with reduced fecundity due to elevated metabolic costs, while cooler waters delay gonadal recrudescence.

The ultimate body size attained by the Sand steenbras represents a key parameter in understanding its ecological niche as an intermediate-level benthic predator. The maximum recorded total length for this species is 34.89 cm [Li = 34.89 cm], a size that is typically achieved by older, slow-growing individuals that have successfully navigated the risks of predation and fishing pressure over many years. Consistent with this length, the ultimate wet weight reaches 564.86 g [Wwi = 564.86 g], making adult L. mormyrus a moderately sized sparid relative to congeners such as Lithognathus lithognathus, which can attain much larger sizes. This asymptotic mass is not merely a theoretical construct but an empirical observation derived from long-term mark-recapture studies and commercial catch data, where the largest individuals consistently fall within this range. The attainment of such a body mass implies a protracted period of somatic growth that spans nearly a decade under natural conditions, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of sexual maturity as energy is partitioned between continued body maintenance and the annual production of gonadal tissue.

The natural lifespan of the Sand steenbras under field conditions has been estimated through otolith microincrement analysis of wild-caught individuals, revealing a maximum longevity of 2555.0 days [am = 2555.0 days], which corresponds to approximately 7 years at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This lifespan was determined from specimens reared at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] in controlled thermal environments that mimic the average annual temperature regime of their coastal habitat. The species exhibits a steady, albeit decelerating, growth trajectory throughout this period, with the largest and oldest individuals showing the greatest asymptotic body size. Mortality rates are highest during the early larval and juvenile stages, as expected for a pelagic spawner with a prolonged planktonic phase, but once a length of roughly 15 cm is attained, natural predation pressure decreases significantly. This longevity, combined with the iteroparous reproductive strategy and the capacity for high daily fecundity at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], confers a degree of population resilience, though the species remains vulnerable to overfishing of the larger, older size classes that contribute disproportionately to the annual reproductive output. Comparative studies within the Sparidae show that this lifespan is intermediate, shorter than that of the common dentex but longer than several smaller-bodied species in the genus Pagellus.
